items.title: Railway Security Incident: Hackers May Have Accessed Customer Environment Variables
items.summary: Railway has disclosed a security incident in which an unauthorized third party may have accessed customer environment variables, including some decrypted values. The cloud platform warned that the affected data could contain API keys, database passwords, and private registry credentials, and urged all customers to replace stored secrets. The company published its security disclosure on October 21, 2026, after detecting unusual activity in systems that store these variables. Its initial findings suggest that only some users may be affected. However, Railway has not released an affected account count, identified the attacker, or explained how access was gained. Railway Security Incident Environment variables hold settings that applications need during builds and normal operation. Railway’s documentation explains that these values can include configuration details and secrets supplied to services. This makes the storage system a sensitive target because stolen credentials could give attackers access to connected services beyond Railway itself. The key distinction is that Railway reported possible access to encrypted variables and, for some, decrypted contents. This does not establish that attackers broke the encryption. The notice does not explain how readable values may have been obtained, leaving that part of the investigation unresolved. Railway believes the incident forms part of a recent series of attacks against platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers. These providers run AI models in response to user requests. Railway said it notified upstream providers and asked them to revoke keys proactively, but did not identify those providers. The suspected focus on AI access reflects a wider credential theft risk. Cybersecurity News previously covered an LLMjacking attack involving a leaked AWS key , where stolen access was used to run paid AI models at the victim’s expense. Railway has not confirmed that similar misuse occurred in this incident. Related reporting on AI agents exposing API keys and cloud secrets also shows why secret handling matters across modern development tools. That report describes exposure through configuration files, command output, and model context. It is background on credential risk, not evidence of how attackers entered Railway’s systems in this case. Deployments Paused as Credential Resets Continue Railway paused deployments during its investigation, preventing customers from releasing new application versions. Its incident status page confirmed that builds remained unavailable at 02:19 UTC on October 22. The restriction also affects recovery because some credential changes require services to be redeployed before applications can use the replacement values. The company also began rotating all Railway storage bucket credentials as a precaution. Replacement credentials will appear automatically in customer dashboards. However, Railway said applications cannot be redeployed to pick up those credentials until builds return, creating an additional recovery hurdle for customers with services that depend on storage buckets. Railway recommends immediately rotating all secrets stored as environment variables, including API keys and private registry credentials, and checking connected service logs for unusual activity. Customers should not wait for confirmation that their account was affected. The company has published guides covering database passwords, AI provider usage, cloud access, and GitHub activity. Railway said it will email customers directly as affected accounts are confirmed. The investigation remains ongoing, with the full scope still unclear. The cloud platform warned that the affected data could contain API keys, database passwords, and private registry credentials, and urged all customers to replace stored secrets.

Railway Security Incident

Environment variables hold settings that applications need during builds and normal operation. Railway’s documentation explains that these values can include configuration details and secrets supplied to services. This makes the storage system a sensitive target because stolen credentials could give attackers access to connected services beyond Railway itself.

The key distinction is that Railway reported possible access to encrypted variables and, for some, decrypted contents. This does not establish that attackers broke the encryption. The notice does not explain how readable values may have been obtained, leaving that part of the investigation unresolved.

Railway believes the incident forms part of a recent series of attacks against platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers. These providers run AI models in response to user requests. Railway said it notified upstream providers and asked them to revoke keys proactively, but did not identify those providers.

The suspected focus on AI access reflects a wider credential theft risk. Cybersecurity News previously covered an LLMjacking attack involving a leaked AWS key, where stolen access was used to run paid AI models at the victim’s expense. Railway has not confirmed that similar misuse occurred in this incident.

Related reporting on AI agents exposing API keys and cloud secrets also shows why secret handling matters across modern development tools. That report describes exposure through configuration files, command output, and model context. It is background on credential risk, not evidence of how attackers entered Railway’s systems in this case.

Railway paused deployments during its investigation, preventing customers from releasing new application versions. items.title: 12-Year-Old GitLab Vulnerability Allows Remote Code Execution on Self-Managed Server
items.summary: GitLab has released urgent security updates for a critical vulnerability that could let attackers run code on self-managed servers without logging in. Tracked as CVE-2026-110264, the flaw carries the maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and affects both GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. The company published the fixes on October 21, 2026. The affected code reaches back to GitLab 7.0, released in 2014, giving the vulnerability a roughly 12-year history. That does not mean attackers have been using it for 12 years. GitLab’s advisory describes the risk but does not report confirmed attacks or provide a public exploit. GitLab Remote Code Execution Flaw According to GitLab’s official security advisory , the vulnerability involves an integer overflow when the server compiles a specially crafted regular expression. Regular expressions are patterns used to match text. Under certain conditions, processing an attacker-controlled pattern could allow arbitrary code to run on the server. GitLab’s CVSS assessment describes a network-based attack with low complexity, no account privileges, and no required user interaction. It rates the possible impact on data privacy, data integrity, and service availability as high. However, the company has not disclosed the full conditions needed to reach the vulnerable code. GitLab credited security researcher joaxcar with reporting the issue through its HackerOne bug bounty program. Its release notes also list Ruby regular-expression patches, providing further context about the affected software layer without revealing a complete attack path. Administrators should not assume the flaw requires access to a particular project or feature unless GitLab confirms that restriction. CVE ID Severity CVSS Score Affected Edition Vulnerability and Potential Impact CVE-2026-110264 Critical 10.0 CE and EE An integer overflow while compiling a specially crafted regular expression could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the GitLab server. CVE-2026-15723 High 8.2 CE and EE Improper input handling during OmniAuth-to-LDAP account linking could let an authenticated attacker take over an LDAP-backed account when SAML and LDAP auto-linking are enabled. CVE-2026-112212 High 7.5 CE and EE Cache poisoning in OAuth/OIDC discovery responses could let an unauthenticated attacker redirect certain authentication flows to an attacker-controlled server. CVE-2026-12664 Medium 6.8 CE and EE Missing GraphQL scope checks could allow a user with a read_api token to retrieve a project’s incoming email address and create work items beyond the token’s intended permissions. CVE-2026-16255 Medium 5.9 EE Incomplete SAML/LDAP membership-lock enforcement could allow authenticated users to grant or accept memberships outside identity-provider controls through requests created before the lock was enabled. CVE-2026-105777 Medium 4.3 CE and EE Improper filtering of internal response headers could expose sensitive internal server credentials under certain conditions. CVE-2026-13319 Medium 4.3 CE and EE Missing authorization checks in the group milestones API could let authenticated users read milestone details and project paths from private projects without membership. CVE-2026-112378 Medium 4.3 EE Insufficient server-side billing checks could allow authenticated users to access paid AI features without a valid subscription. CVE-2026-105711 Low 3.5 CE and EE Incorrect caching of merge request titles could expose confidential issue titles to authenticated users without project membership. CVE-2026-14288 Low 3.1 EE Improper access control during approval-rule synchronization could allow authenticated users to bypass required merge request approvals on protected branches. CVE-2026-112326 Low 3.1 EE Incorrect cleanup during error handling could allow users with read-only permissions to permanently delete existing vulnerability records. CVE-2026-103515 Low 2.7 EE Incomplete enforcement of a Duo administrator lock could allow group Owners to re-enable AI-backed data transfers to a third-party service through Amazon Q settings. Affected Versions and Available Fixes The vulnerability affects GitLab CE and EE versions starting with 7.0. GitLab has fixed it in versions 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, 19.2.9, 19.3.6, 19.4.3, and 19.5.1. Earlier releases within those branches remain affected. The company extended the fix to four older branches beyond its standard patch releases. Self-managed customers should upgrade immediately. GitLab.com already runs patched software. GitLab Dedicated tenants running 19.3.5-internal0, 19.4.2-internal0, or later already include the fixes and require no action, according to the notice. GitLab also says that when an advisory does not name a specific deployment type, all deployment types are affected. This issue should not be confused with the earlier GitLab code execution vulnerability patched on October 12. That separate flaw, CVE-2026-97229, also involved regular-expression handling but affected a different version range. Installing that earlier update does not address this newly disclosed vulnerability. GitLab has published two detection guides for self-managed environments, named “Onigmo native worker crash” and “Org mode render error burst.” These resources are intended to help security teams identify possible exploitation attempts. Their publication is not evidence that attacks have occurred, and the release notice does not establish either signal as proof of a successful compromise. The patch release addresses 12 vulnerabilities overall. Another serious issue, CVE-2026-15723, carries a CVSS score of 8.2. When OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking are both enabled, an authenticated attacker could take over an existing LDAP-backed account without the victim’s involvement. CVE-2026-112212, rated 7.5, concerns poisoned OAuth and OpenID Connect discovery responses that could redirect certain flows to an attacker-controlled server. These fixes follow other recent GitLab security updates, including a separate AI Gateway remote command execution vulnerability . Those reports concern different components and attack requirements, making accurate version checks more useful than assuming one GitLab update covers every related product. Administrators should review GitLab’s upgrade instructions before deployment. The notice warns that database migrations can affect the process, with downtime for single-node installations and zero-downtime procedures available for suitable multi-node setups. Versions 19.3.6 and 19.4.3 include regular migrations. GitLab normally makes detailed security issues public 90 days after patching, so teams should not delay updates while waiting for full technical details. The GitLab fixes arrive alongside security updates for Node.js and PHP, adding to the patching workload for teams running web applications and development services. Cyber Security News reports that Node.js released security updates addressing ten vulnerabilities across its 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x branches, with patched versions listed as 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4. Meanwhile, PHP issued emergency patches for PHP2Shell , a pair of critical memory-handling flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. items.title: GoDaddy Revoking 404,607 TLS Certificates Following Compliance Failures
items.summary: GoDaddy launched a mass revocation of 404,607 SSL/TLS certificates after finding that issued certificates did not match its published certificate policies. The company missed its required revocation deadline, creating a second compliance issue. An updated customer notice says the incorrectly issued certificates were revoked on October 21, 2026. The incident affects certificates issued under GoDaddy and Starfield certificate chains. Customers still using an affected certificate may face browser security warnings or website access problems until they install a replacement, according to GoDaddy’s customer guidance . Receiving a replacement alone does not confirm that the website is using it. GoDaddy Revoking 404,607 TLS Certificates According to the original incident report , a third party flagged differences between issued certificates and the profiles described in Starfield’s Certificate Policy and Certification Practice Statement, known as CP/CPS. These documents set out the rules the certificate authority follows when issuing certificates. The differences involved certificate policy information, including policy object identifiers, or OIDs, and CPS URI policy qualifiers. These fields identify certificate policies and reference the authority’s published practices. The issued certificates did not match the documented profiles. The reports describe a compliance failure, not a confirmed theft of private keys. GoDaddy stopped certificate issuance after confirming the report. Its investigation uncovered additional differences across affected profiles. The company corrected and published its documentation before resuming issuance. Further checks found similar problems in the older Starfield G2 chain, which was no longer actively issuing certificates. Domain validated certificates made up most of the affected population. Starfield R1 DV accounted for 208,896 certificates, while Starfield G2 DV accounted for 187,159. Smaller numbers of organization validated and extended validation certificates were also affected across the GoDaddy and Starfield chains. GoDaddy Missed the Revocation Deadline The delayed revocation report cites Section 4.9.1.1 of the TLS Baseline Requirements. For the stated policy violation, affected certificates should be revoked within 24 hours and must be revoked within five days, except for short-lived subscriber certificates. The specified revocation reason is “superseded.” GoDaddy began contacting subscribers on October 14. Its outreach included customers holding large certificate inventories and organizations providing government, financial, and health services. However, only 170,566 certificates had been revoked when the October 18 deadline passed at 23:45 UTC. By 05:29 UTC on October 19, the revoked total had reached 227,422. GoDaddy said dedicated teams were handling customer contact, replacement, revocation, and progress tracking through email, SMS, and phone calls. Its later customer notice states that the incorrectly issued certificates were revoked on October 21. Affected administrators should review the SSL certificate section of their GoDaddy account and follow any replacement notice. GoDaddy warns that an updated certificate can exist in the account while the domain continues serving the old certificate. Customers receiving an installation alert should download and install the replacement immediately. The case echoes earlier DigiCert certificate revocations following a DNS validation error , although the underlying failures differ. It also highlights the operational concerns covered in Cybersecurity News’ report on certificate mismanagement . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Using AWS WAF to apply mitigations for PHP2Shell RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)
items.summary: On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released emergency fixes for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in the PHP core runtime, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively named PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, and both allow an unauthenticated attacker to run code on a vulnerable server. The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority. But patching a fleet takes time: you need to inventory where PHP runs, schedule maintenance windows and test applications against the new builds. This post shows you how to use AWS Web Application Firewall ( AWS WAF ) to help reduce exposure to the confirmed attack paths during that window. You’ll learn which request patterns to block, how to write the rules in AWS WAFv2, how to deploy them without breaking legitimate traffic and where its protection ends, so you don’t develop a false sense of safety. For how Amazon threat intelligence detected PHP2Shell exploitation before public disclosure, see Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot . For AWS service status and the AWS WAF rule that AWS recommends, see AWS Security Bulletin 2026-143-AWS . IMPORTANT: Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority. The vulnerabilities in brief Both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are unauthenticated RCE issues rooted in how PHP handles multipart/form-data request processing (the request format browsers use for file uploads) before your application code runs, which is why the AWS WAF rules in this post focus on multipart traffic, request body size, and the session upload progress field. At a high level, CVE-2026-109618 corrupts memory when PHP runs out of memory mid-request, and CVE-2026-109619 lets one request leave behind stale data that a later request on the same worker process reuses. For the root-cause analysis, affected versions, and PHP’s own guidance, see the official PHP advisories and release announcement: CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) – PHP advisory GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state) – PHP advisory GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp PHP security release announcement, October 21, 2026 Where AWS WAF fits in your response AWS WAF is a defense-in-depth control in this situation, not a replacement for the PHP upgrade. The PHP advisories are explicit: updating to a patched release is the only complete mitigation. One of the two vulnerabilities is largely outside the reach of any web application firewall, as explained later. Treat the rules in this post as mitigating controls that help reduce exposure while you patch, then remove them or keep them as supporting controls after you’ve patched. AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests at the edge. It doesn’t parse the internal structure of a multipart body, and it has no visibility into PHP worker memory or server-side configuration. The following table maps each attack element to whether AWS WAF can help mitigate it. Attack element AWS WAF coverage Session upload progress field in a multipart POST ( PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS , the form field that turns on PHP’s upload-tracking feature) Yes. A targeted rule can block requests carrying that field. Multipart upload path ( multipart/form-data , the request type used for file uploads and the entry point for both vulnerabilities) Yes, if the application has no legitimate multipart uploads. Block multipart/form-data. Out-of-memory condition from an oversized body Partial. Cap the request body size. Doesn’t catch header amplification (many small part headers that cost far more memory to represent than their size on the wire) that stays under the cap. Repeated attempts against the same worker (the reused PHP process that handles many requests) Yes. A rate-based rule blunts the volume an exploit needs. fatal_error_backtraces producer (a PHP 8.5 setting that stores crash-trace state across a request) No. This is a server configuration setting ( fatal_error_backtraces=0 ). Invalid or deprecated INI diagnostics as a consumer (warnings PHP raises when applying bad configuration settings) No. This path runs server-side, not over client HTTP. Where an application does not accept multipart uploads, an edge rule that blocks multipart/form-data removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application, plus the session-upload-progress trigger, which is a defense-in-depth control during the patch window. If your application does use multipart uploads, AWS WAF reduces risk but does not close the vulnerability, because header amplification (a few kilobytes of part headers that expand into far more memory inside PHP) stays within size limits and the firewall cannot parse the headers inside individual body parts. In that case, prioritize the PHP upgrade and apply the server-side mitigations described later. Implementing the AWS WAF rules The rules below are AWS WAFv2 JSON, deploy each of them on the WAF protection pack (web ACL) associated with the Amazon CloudFront distribution, Application Load Balancer, or Amazon API Gateway stage in front of your PHP workloads. IMPORTANT: Before implementing any changes, ensure that your WAFv2 logging is setup in line with AWS WAF Logging guidance. Start every rule in Count mode, confirm it does not match legitimate traffic, then switch to Block. Request body inspection limits AWS WAF inspects a bounded portion of the request body. On Application Load Balancer and AWS AppSync the limit is a fixed 8 KB. For AWS services such as CloudFront and API Gateway, the default is 16 KB and you can raise it to 32, 48, or 64 KB through the web ACL AssociationConfig as seen below. Any part of the body beyond the inspection limit counts as oversize. Choose the limit that fits the rules you deploy, because a body-size rule can only enforce a cap up to the inspected size. aws wafv2 update-web-acl ... --association-config \ 'RequestBody={CLOUDFRONT={DefaultSizeInspectionLimit=KB_16}}' AWS WAF Rule This rule targets both CVEs by blocking a request only when all three conditions in its AndStatement are true at once: The method is exactly POST – matched on the HTTP method, no transformation. A PHP session identifier is present (the nested OrStatement , so either sub-condition satisfies this leg): PHPSESSID appears as a cookie key (exact match on the key, scanning all cookies), or PHPSESSID appears anywhere in the request body (contains match). The body contains PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS – the form field that activates PHP’s session upload progress feature. items.summary_html:
On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released emergency fixes for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in the PHP core runtime, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively named PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, and both allow an unauthenticated attacker to run code on a vulnerable server. The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority. But patching a fleet takes time: you need to inventory where PHP runs, schedule maintenance windows and test applications against the new builds. This post shows you how to use AWS Web Application Firewall (AWS WAF) to help reduce exposure to the confirmed attack paths during that window. You’ll learn which request patterns to block, how to write the rules in AWS WAFv2, how to deploy them without breaking legitimate traffic and where its protection ends, so you don’t develop a false sense of safety. For how Amazon threat intelligence detected PHP2Shell exploitation before public disclosure, see Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot. For AWS service status and the AWS WAF rule that AWS recommends, see AWS Security Bulletin 2026-143-AWS.

IMPORTANT: Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority.

The vulnerabilities in brief

Both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are unauthenticated RCE issues rooted in how PHP handles multipart/form-data request processing (the request format browsers use for file uploads) before your application code runs, which is why the AWS WAF rules in this post focus on multipart traffic, request body size, and the session upload progress field. At a high level, CVE-2026-109618 corrupts memory when PHP runs out of memory mid-request, and CVE-2026-109619 lets one request leave behind stale data that a later request on the same worker process reuses. For the root-cause analysis, affected versions, and PHP’s own guidance, see the official PHP advisories and release announcement:

  • CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) – PHP advisory GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w
  • CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state) – PHP advisory GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp
  • PHP security release announcement, October 21, 2026
Where AWS WAF fits in your response

AWS WAF is a defense-in-depth control in this situation, not a replacement for the PHP upgrade. The PHP advisories are explicit: updating to a patched release is the only complete mitigation. One of the two vulnerabilities is largely outside the reach of any web application firewall, as explained later. Treat the rules in this post as mitigating controls that help reduce exposure while you patch, then remove them or keep them as supporting controls after you’ve patched.

AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests at the edge. It doesn’t parse the internal structure of a multipart body, and it has no visibility into PHP worker memory or server-side configuration. The following table maps each attack element to whether AWS WAF can help mitigate it.

Attack element

AWS WAF coverage

Session upload progress field in a multipart POST (PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS, the form field that turns on PHP’s upload-tracking feature)

Yes. A targeted rule can block requests carrying that field.

Multipart upload path (multipart/form-data, the request type used for file uploads and the entry point for both vulnerabilities)

Yes, if the application has no legitimate multipart uploads. Block multipart/form-data.

Out-of-memory condition from an oversized body

Partial. Cap the request body size. Doesn’t catch header amplification (many small part headers that cost far more memory to represent than their size on the wire) that stays under the cap.

Repeated attempts against the same worker (the reused PHP process that handles many requests)

Yes. A rate-based rule blunts the volume an exploit needs.

fatal_error_backtraces producer (a PHP 8.5 setting that stores crash-trace state across a request)

No. This is a server configuration setting (fatal_error_backtraces=0).

Invalid or deprecated INI diagnostics as a consumer (warnings PHP raises when applying bad configuration settings)

No. This path runs server-side, not over client HTTP.

Where an application does not accept multipart uploads, an edge rule that blocks multipart/form-data removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application, plus the session-upload-progress trigger, which is a defense-in-depth control during the patch window.

If your application does use multipart uploads, AWS WAF reduces risk but does not close the vulnerability, because header amplification (a few kilobytes of part headers that expand into far more memory inside PHP) stays within size limits and the firewall cannot parse the headers inside individual body parts. In that case, prioritize the PHP upgrade and apply the server-side mitigations described later.

Implementing the AWS WAF rules

The rules below are AWS WAFv2 JSON, deploy each of them on the WAF protection pack (web ACL) associated with the Amazon CloudFront distribution, Application Load Balancer, or Amazon API Gateway stage in front of your PHP workloads.

IMPORTANT: Before implementing any changes, ensure that your WAFv2 logging is setup in line with AWS WAF Logging guidance. Start every rule in Count mode, confirm it does not match legitimate traffic, then switch to Block.

Request body inspection limits

AWS WAF inspects a bounded portion of the request body. On Application Load Balancer and AWS AppSync the limit is a fixed 8 KB. For AWS services such as CloudFront and API Gateway, the default is 16 KB and you can raise it to 32, 48, or 64 KB through the web ACL AssociationConfig as seen below. Any part of the body beyond the inspection limit counts as oversize. Choose the limit that fits the rules you deploy, because a body-size rule can only enforce a cap up to the inspected size.

aws wafv2 update-web-acl ... --association-config \
'RequestBody={CLOUDFRONT={DefaultSizeInspectionLimit=KB_16}}'

AWS WAF Rule

This rule targets both CVEs by blocking a request only when all three conditions in its AndStatement are true at once:

  1. The method is exactly POST – matched on the HTTP method, no transformation.
  2. A PHP session identifier is present (the nested OrStatement, so either sub-condition satisfies this leg):

    • PHPSESSID appears as a cookie key (exact match on the key, scanning all cookies), or
    • PHPSESSID appears anywhere in the request body (contains match).
  3. The body contains PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS – the form field that activates PHP’s session upload progress feature.

Pair the rule with session.upload_progress.enabled=0 on the server, which turns the feature off.

{
  "Name": "PHP2Shell",
  "Priority": 0,
  "Statement": {
    "AndStatement": {
      "Statements": [
        {
          "ByteMatchStatement": {
            "SearchString": "POST",
            "FieldToMatch": {
              "Method": {}
            },
            "TextTransformations": [
              {
                "Priority": 0,
                "Type": "NONE"
              }
            ],
            "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY"
          }
        },
        {
          "OrStatement": {
            "Statements": [
              {
                "ByteMatchStatement": {
                  "SearchString": "PHPSESSID",
                  "FieldToMatch": {
                    "Cookies": {
                      "MatchPattern": {
                        "All": {}
                      },
                      "MatchScope": "KEY",
                      "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE"
                    }
                  },
                  "TextTransformations": [
                    {
                      "Priority": 0,
                      "Type": "NONE"
                    }
                  ],
                  "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY"
                }
              },
              {
                "ByteMatchStatement": {
                  "SearchString": "PHPSESSID",
                  "FieldToMatch": {
                    "Body": {
                      "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE"
                    }
                  },
                  "TextTransformations": [
                    {
                      "Priority": 0,
                      "Type": "NONE"
                    }
                  ],
                  "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS"
                }
              }
            ]
          }
        },
        {
          "ByteMatchStatement": {
            "SearchString": "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS",
            "FieldToMatch": {
              "Body": {
                "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE"
              }
            },
            "TextTransformations": [
              {
                "Priority": 0,
                "Type": "NONE"
              }
            ],
            "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS"
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "Action": {
    "Block": {}
  },
  "VisibilityConfig": {
    "SampledRequestsEnabled": true,
    "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true,
    "MetricName": "PHP2Shell"
  }
}

Additional WAF Rules to consider

Block multipart requests when the application has no uploads

NOTE: This rule, if implemented in Block mode, will break applications that require file uploads. If your application does not require file uploads, then blocking multipart/form-data removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application for both CVEs at the edge.

A single named header is inspected in full, with no 8 KB header cap, so matching the Content-Type header is reliable.

{
  "Name": "Block-Multipart-FormData",
  "Priority": 1,
  "Action": { "Count": {} },
  "Statement": {
    "ByteMatchStatement": {
      "FieldToMatch": { "SingleHeader": { "Name": "content-type" } },
      "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS",
      "SearchString": "multipart/form-data",
      "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "LOWERCASE" } ]
    }
  },
  "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBlockMultipart" }
}

Cap the request body size

Capping body size reduces the out-of-memory condition behind CVE-2026-109618 and the stale state it can leave behind. Use OversizeHandling: MATCH with a size constraint so that any body larger than the threshold is blocked, including bodies that exceed the inspection limit. To enforce a cap of N bytes, the web ACL body inspection limit must be at least N. Note that you can’t cap the numeric Content-Length with a size constraint, because the constraint measures the length of the header value string, not the number it contains. If your application has legitimate large uploads, scope this rule to non-upload paths with an AndStatement on the URI path, or it will break those uploads.

{
  "Name": "Block-Oversize-Body",
  "Priority": 3,
  "Action": { "Count": {} },
  "Statement": {
    "SizeConstraintStatement": {
      "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "MATCH" } },
      "ComparisonOperator": "GT",
      "Size": 8192,
      "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ]
    }
  },
  "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellBlockOversizeBody" }
}

NOTE: if you already have the AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet managed rule group, the SizeRestrictions_BODY rule blocks bodies larger than 8 KB by default. If a specific managed rule breaks legitimate traffic, override that rule to Count rather than disabling the whole group.

Rate-limit repeated attempts

A rate-based rule on POST requests can reduce the volume an attacker can send, lowering the possibility that the vulnerabilities can be triggered by overloading the worker, while the stale-state path needs a producer request and a consumer request to land on the same worker. This rule complements a server setting of pm.max_requests=1, which recycles the worker on each request.

{
  "Name": "RateLimit-Posts",
  "Priority": 4,
  "Action": { "Count": {} },
  "Statement": {
    "RateBasedStatement": {
      "Limit": 100,
      "EvaluationWindowSec": 60,
      "AggregateKeyType": "IP",
      "ScopeDownStatement": {
        "ByteMatchStatement": {
          "FieldToMatch": { "Method": {} },
          "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY",
          "SearchString": "POST",
          "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ]
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2ShellRateLimitPosts" }
}

Server-side mitigations that complement AWS WAF

These host and runtime changes address the parts of CVE-2026-109619 that sit below the HTTP layer a WAF inspects, so they fall outside its scope by design. Apply them alongside the AWS WAF rules as the host and runtime layer of your defense.

  • Upgrade PHP to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. This is the only complete fix. PHP 8.1 and earlier are no longer supported upstream, so check with your distribution or long-term support vendor for a backported fix, or plan a move to a supported branch.
  • Address CVE-2026-109618 at the PHP level. Set memory_limit=-1 so applications cannot override it, and keep post_max_size low (8M where the application accepts no uploads, 32M where it does). Enforce memory bounds through container or cgroup limits, never through RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which trigger the vulnerable out-of-memory path.
  • Set fatal_error_backtraces=0 on PHP 8.5 and restart every worker. This disables the setting that stores crash-trace state across a request, one of the confirmed ways the vulnerability is triggered.
  • Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. This turns off the upload-tracking feature that’s the other confirmed trigger, and is prudent to keep off even after patching.
  • Prefer php.ini, FPM pool, or server startup configuration over per-request INI overrides (settings applied per request through .htaccess, php_value, or FastCGI PHP_VALUE). Remove obsolete directives so they don’t raise diagnostic warnings.
  • Eliminate fatal errors and execution timeouts on attacker-reachable routes, including upload, import, error-page, shutdown, serialization, and extension paths.
  • Set pm.max_requests=1 if performance allows, so each worker process is recycled after one request, which breaks the link between the request that plants stale data and a later request that would reuse it.
  • Turn on error logging (log_errors=On, a working error_log, error_reporting=E_ALL) and review your Apache, FPM, or proxy logs for repeated warnings, deprecations, fatal errors, and timeouts on attacker-controlled routes. The absence of errors is not proof of safety.
Getting started

Complete the following steps to get started:

  1. Inventory where PHP runs and which versions and server APIs (mod_php, FPM, FrankenPHP, LSAPI) are in use. Identify any public endpoint that accepts a request body.
  2. Decide whether each application uses multipart uploads. This determines whether you can deploy the WAF rule to block multipart requests.
  3. Create or update the web ACL in front of each PHP workload and add the applicable rules in Count mode. Raise the body inspection limit on CloudFront or API Gateway if a rule needs it.
  4. Watch the sampled requests and Amazon CloudWatch metrics for each rule. Confirm that legitimate uploads and large JSON POSTs aren’t matched.
  5. Switch the rules to Block after the metrics are clean. Order the priorities so the session upload progress and multipart rules run before the size and rate rules.
  6. Test with a benign multipart/form-data POST, an oversized body, and a request carrying PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS. Expect a 403 response and the matching rule metric.
  7. In parallel, apply the PHP upgrade and the configuration mitigations. Remove or retain the AWS WAF rules as supporting controls after your fleet is patched.
Conclusion

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities—CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619—are unauthenticated RCE vulnerabilities that reach PHP before your application code runs. AWS WAF gives you a way to help narrow the attack surface during the patch window: block the session upload progress field, block multipart requests where no uploads are expected, cap request body size, and rate-limit repeated attempts. These mitigating controls can help reduce exposure, but they don’t close the vulnerabilities. Upgrade PHP to a fixed release, apply the server configuration changes, and treat the AWS WAF rules as the edge layer that supports those fixes rather than the fix itself.

To learn more about the rule types used here, see the AWS WAF documentation on the web ACL body inspection limit, oversize request component handling, and handling oversize HTTP request bodies. For the vulnerability details, see the PHP advisories GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w and GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp, and the PHP session upload progress manual.
